articles.title: Airplane trails trap heat, but we can easily halve them
articles.excerpt: When you watch planes in the sky, more often than not you’ll see white trails form behind them. They start as thin lines, then spread into larger artificial clouds that trap heat. These so-called contrails form when the hot, moist exhaust from a plane's engines meets the cold air of the upper atmosphere. The water vapour instantly freezes into tiny ice crystals, and that's the white line you see. Contrails warm the planet the same way CO₂ does: they absorb heat radiating off the Earth and reflect it back down. The key difference is longevity. While CO₂ lingers in the atmosphere for centuries, contrails disappear within hours. Planes fly every single day, constantly producing new ones. In 2019, the accumulated warming from all those short-lived contrails added up to roughly the same warming as all the lingering CO₂ from aviation emitted since 1940. articles.title: Plenty of krill in the sea
articles.excerpt: German drugstore giant dm, with 4,000 stores across Europe, just dropped krill from its shelves, following Holland & Barrett’s similar announcement for the UK market. Krill are about as big as your finger is wide, but almost nothing in the Southern Ocean survives without them. They are the single link converting phytoplankton energy into food for other species. “This species plays a central role in the Southern Ocean ecosystem,” Antarctic researcher Bettina Meyer told The European Correspondent. “It is the primary food source for iconic predators in the Southern Ocean such as baleen whales, penguins, seals, and seabirds.” Scientific evidence suggests krill populations around the Antarctic Peninsula have declined by as much as 80% since the 1970s, with sea ice loss and fishery being the main threats.
